prompt: Air brakes are really three braking systems in one. Which three?
choices: Service, engine retarder, and trailer brakes
Primary, secondary, and spring brakes
Service, parking, and emergency brakes
Foot, hand, and exhaust brakes
explanation: The manual describes air brakes as three systems: the service brake (pedal), the parking brake (parking control), and the emergency brake, which uses parts of the other two when the system fails.

prompt: What does the air compressor do?
choices: Pumps air into the air storage tanks
Sends air from the tanks to the brake chambers
Controls when the tanks are drained
Turns the brake lights on when you brake
explanation: The air compressor pumps air into the air storage tanks (reservoirs). It is driven by the engine through gears or a V-belt.

prompt: The air compressor on your truck has its own oil supply. What should you do before driving?
choices: Drain the compressor oil into the air tanks
Add alcohol to the compressor oil
Nothing; it is lubricated by engine oil
Check the compressor's oil level
explanation: A compressor may have its own oil supply or use engine oil. If it has its own supply, check that oil level before driving.

prompt: What part controls when the air compressor pumps air into the storage tanks?
choices: The safety relief valve
The air compressor governor
The tractor protection valve
The foot (treadle) valve
explanation: The governor stops the compressor at the cut-out pressure and lets it start pumping again at the cut-in pressure.

prompt: At about what tank pressure does the governor stop the compressor from pumping (cut-out)?
choices: About 100 psi
About 125 psi
About 150 psi
About 85 psi
explanation: The cut-out level is around 125 psi. About 100 psi is the cut-in level, and 150 psi is where the safety valve usually opens.

prompt: At about what tank pressure does the governor let the compressor start pumping again (cut-in)?
choices: About 55 psi
About 125 psi
About 60 psi
About 100 psi
explanation: When tank pressure falls to the cut-in pressure, around 100 psi, the governor lets the compressor start pumping again.

prompt: How much air do the air storage tanks hold if the compressor stops working?
choices: Enough to use the brakes several times
Enough to drive about 100 more miles at highway speed
Only enough for one brake application
Enough to refill the tires once
explanation: The tanks hold enough air to let you use the brakes several times, even if the compressor stops working.

prompt: Why must air tanks be drained?
choices: To release extra pressure that the governor failed to stop
To let the alcohol evaporator refill them with fresh alcohol
Water and oil collect in them and can cause brake failure
To lower the pressure so the compressor can cool down
explanation: Compressed air carries water and oil that collect at the bottom of the tanks. Water can freeze in cold weather and cause brake failure.

prompt: Your air tanks have manual drain valves. How often must you drain them?
choices: Once a week, or every 1,000 miles
Only in freezing weather
Only when the safety valve opens
At the end of each day of driving
explanation: With manually operated drains, you must drain the tanks yourself at the end of each day of driving.

prompt: What is the purpose of an alcohol evaporator in an air brake system?
choices: To clean compressor oil out of the air tanks each day
To cool the brake drums on long, steep downgrades
To reduce the risk of ice in the air system in cold weather
To replace the need for draining the air tanks
explanation: An alcohol evaporator puts alcohol into the air system to reduce the risk of ice forming in brake valves and other parts during cold weather.

prompt: In cold weather, how often should you check and fill the alcohol container?
choices: Once a week
Every day
Every 1,000 miles
Only when the warning light comes on
explanation: Check the alcohol container and fill it as necessary every day during cold weather.

prompt: Your truck has an alcohol evaporator but manual tank drains. What is true about draining the tanks?
choices: You still need to drain the tanks daily to remove water and oil
Draining is not needed because the alcohol absorbs the water
Drain only when temperatures fall below freezing
Drain once a week instead of daily
explanation: The evaporator only helps prevent ice. Daily tank draining is still needed to get rid of water and oil unless the system has automatic drains.

prompt: Where is the safety relief valve installed?
choices: In the first tank the compressor pumps air to
In the last tank on the trailer, farthest from the compressor
On each brake chamber, next to the slack adjuster
On the dashboard, next to the supply pressure gauges
explanation: A safety relief valve is installed in the first tank the compressor pumps air to, protecting the system from too much pressure.

prompt: The safety relief valve is usually set to open at about:
choices: 125 psi
150 psi
100 psi
175 psi
explanation: The safety valve is usually set to open at 150 psi. About 125 psi is the normal governor cut-out.

prompt: You hear the safety relief valve releasing air. What should you conclude?
choices: It is normal; the valve vents each time the governor cuts in
The tanks need to be drained right away
Something is wrong, and a mechanic should fix the fault
The alcohol evaporator is empty
explanation: If the safety valve releases air, something is wrong. Have the fault fixed by a mechanic; the valve should not vent during normal operation.

prompt: What are two other names for the air brake pedal?
choices: Trolley valve or Johnson bar
Relay valve or quick-release valve
Modulating valve or limiting valve
Foot valve or treadle valve
explanation: The brake pedal is also called the foot valve or treadle valve. The trolley valve (Johnson bar) is the trailer hand valve.

prompt: What happens when you push the air brake pedal down harder?
choices: The governor cuts in sooner to refill the tanks
Air is released from the spring brakes
More air pressure is applied to the brakes
The compressor pumps faster
explanation: Pushing the pedal down harder applies more air pressure; letting up reduces pressure and releases the brakes.

prompt: Why can pressing and releasing the brake pedal over and over (fanning) be dangerous while driving?
choices: It overheats the governor and makes it stop working
It makes the safety relief valve stick in the open position
It uses up the alcohol in the evaporator too quickly
It can drain air faster than the compressor refills it
explanation: Each release lets some compressed air out of the system. Unnecessary fanning can drop pressure faster than the compressor refills it, and if pressure gets too low the brakes won't work.

prompt: What is the most common type of foundation brake on air-braked vehicles?
choices: The S-cam drum brake
The wedge brake
The air-operated disc brake
The hydraulic drum brake
explanation: The S-cam drum brake is the most common type. Wedge and disc brakes are less common.

prompt: When you release the brake pedal on an S-cam brake, what pulls the brake shoes away from the drum?
choices: Air pressure from the supply tank pushing them back
A spring, as the S-cam rotates back
The slack adjuster pushing outward
The wheel bearing turning the drum
explanation: When you release the pedal, the S-cam rotates back and a spring pulls the brake shoes away from the drum so the wheels can roll freely.

prompt: In a wedge brake, how are the brake shoes pushed against the drum?
choices: A slack adjuster twists an S-shaped cam against the shoes
A power screw clamps a rotor between two lining pads
A push rod forces a wedge between the shoe ends
Springs push the shoes out when air pressure is removed
explanation: In a wedge brake, the brake chamber push rod pushes a wedge directly between the ends of two brake shoes, shoving them apart and against the drum.

prompt: In an air-operated disc brake, what takes the place of the S-cam?
choices: A power screw
A wedge
A brake drum
A relay valve
explanation: Air disc brakes use a power screw instead of an S-cam. The slack adjuster turns the screw, which clamps the rotor between the pads of a caliper like a large C-clamp.

prompt: What does friction between the brake linings and the drum produce besides slowing the vehicle?
choices: Compressed air
Electric current
Moisture
Heat
explanation: Pressing the shoes and linings against the drum causes friction, which slows the vehicle and creates heat. Too much heat can make the brakes stop working.

prompt: What does the supply pressure gauge tell you?
choices: How much pressure you are applying to the brakes
How much air pressure is in the air tanks
How fast the compressor is turning
How much air is in the tires
explanation: Supply pressure gauges, connected to the air tanks, show how much pressure is in the tanks.

prompt: A vehicle has a dual air brake system. How is supply pressure usually shown?
choices: A single-needle gauge showing both systems combined
One gauge for each half, or one gauge with two needles
Only a warning light, since dual systems have no gauges
A small gauge mounted on each brake chamber
explanation: With a dual air brake system there will be a gauge for each half of the system, or a single gauge with two needles.

prompt: What does the application pressure gauge show?
choices: The amount of air stored in the supply tanks
The pressure at which the governor cuts in
The air pressure in the trailer's tires
The air pressure being applied to the brakes
explanation: The application pressure gauge shows how much air pressure you are applying to the brakes. It is not on all vehicles.

prompt: On a downgrade, you must apply more and more pressure to hold the same speed. What is the most likely cause and response?
choices: The brakes are fading; slow down and use a lower gear
The governor has cut out; keep braking steadily
The ABS is working; keep the same pressure
The tanks are overfilled; fan the brakes to release air
explanation: Increasing application pressure to hold the same speed means the brakes are fading. Slow down and use a lower gear.

prompt: Besides brake fade, what can cause a need for higher application pressure to stop?
choices: Shifting into a lower gear before starting down the grade
Having working ABS on every axle of the vehicle
Brakes out of adjustment, air leaks, or mechanical problems
Keeping the alcohol evaporator full in cold weather
explanation: The need for increased application pressure can also be caused by brakes out of adjustment, air leaks, or mechanical problems.

prompt: Before tank pressure falls below what level must the low air pressure warning come on?
choices: 20 psi
85 psi
100 psi
55 psi
explanation: A visible warning must come on before the air pressure in the tanks falls below 55 psi (or one half the governor cut-out pressure on older vehicles).

prompt: What is the low air pressure warning signal usually?
choices: A yellow light on the left rear of the trailer
A flashing green light
A red light, sometimes with a buzzer
A vibration in the steering wheel
explanation: The warning is usually a red light, and a buzzer may also come on. A yellow lamp is the ABS malfunction lamp.

prompt: What is a "wig wag"?
choices: A spring-loaded dash lever that applies the spring brakes gradually
A mechanical arm that drops into view when pressure falls below 55 psi
A valve that switches air between the primary and secondary tanks
A light on the trailer that flashes while the ABS is working
explanation: A wig wag is a low air warning device that drops a mechanical arm into the driver's view when pressure drops below 55 psi.

prompt: You try to push a manual-reset wig wag out of view, but it keeps dropping back. Why?
choices: It won't stay up until pressure is above 55 psi
The governor has not yet reached the 125 psi cut-out
Manual-reset wig wags can only be reset by a mechanic
The parking brake knob is still pulled out
explanation: A manual-reset wig wag must be placed out of view by hand, and it will not stay in place until the pressure is above 55 psi.

prompt: On large buses, the low pressure warning devices commonly signal at:
explanation: The manual notes that on large buses it is common for low pressure warning devices to signal at 80-85 psi.

prompt: How does an air brake system turn on the brake lights?
choices: With a switch on the parking brake control knob
With an electric switch that works by air pressure
With a sensor that measures brake drum temperature
With a switch connected to the slack adjuster
explanation: An electric stop light switch worked by air pressure turns on the brake lights when you put on the air brakes.

prompt: An older truck (built before 1975) has a front brake limiting valve control. In which position should you keep it?
choices: "Slippery"
"Slippery" on wet roads and "normal" when dry
"Normal"
"Emergency"
explanation: The "slippery" setting cuts front brake air by half and reduces stopping power. Front wheel braking is good under all conditions, so keep the control in "normal."

prompt: What is true about braking with the front wheels on an icy road?
choices: Front brake pressure should be cut in half to prevent skids
Front brakes should be turned off on icy roads
Only the trailer brakes should be used on ice
Front wheel braking is good under all conditions, even on ice
explanation: Tests have shown front wheel skids from braking are not likely even on ice. Limiting front brakes only reduces stopping power.

prompt: Automatic front wheel limiting valves reduce air to the front brakes EXCEPT when:
choices: The road surface is wet, icy, or snow-covered
The driver switches the dash control to "normal"
The brakes are applied very hard (55 psi or more)
The vehicle is traveling at less than 20 mph
explanation: Automatic front limiting valves reduce air to the front brakes except when the brakes are put on very hard (55 psi or more application pressure). The driver cannot control them.

prompt: Why must parking and emergency brakes be held on by mechanical force?
choices: Because air brakes cannot work below freezing
Because ABS needs mechanical brakes to work
Because spring force stops the vehicle faster than air
Because air pressure can eventually leak away
explanation: Emergency and parking brakes must be held on by mechanical force because air pressure can eventually leak away. Spring brakes usually meet this need.

prompt: While you drive, what holds back the powerful springs in spring brakes?
choices: Air pressure
The parking brake lever latch
Hydraulic fluid
The slack adjuster
explanation: When driving, the springs are held back by air pressure. If the air pressure is removed, the springs put on the brakes.

prompt: On tractors and straight trucks, spring brakes come fully on when air pressure drops to:
choices: A range of 55 to 60 psi
A range of 20 to 45 psi
A range of 80 to 85 psi
Exactly 0 psi
explanation: Tractor and straight truck spring brakes come fully on when pressure drops to 20-45 psi (typically 20-30 psi).

prompt: The low air warning light and buzzer come on while you are driving. What should you do?
choices: Keep driving, since the spring brakes will stop you if pressure gets too low
Pump the brake pedal to build pressure back up
Stop safely right away while you can still control the brakes
Drive to the next truck stop before checking
explanation: Do not wait for the spring brakes to come on automatically. When the warning first comes on, bring the vehicle to a safe stop right away while you can still control the brakes.

prompt: If the brakes are badly out of adjustment, what is affected?
choices: The service brakes and the emergency/parking brakes alike
Only the regular service brakes, not the parking brakes
Only the parking brakes, not the service brakes
No brakes at all, because spring brakes adjust themselves
explanation: Spring brake power depends on the brakes being in adjustment. If they are not adjusted properly, neither the regular brakes nor the emergency/parking brakes will work right.

prompt: On newer air-braked vehicles, what does the parking brake control look like?
choices: A red, eight-sided push-pull knob on the dash
A round blue knob
A lever on the steering column
A yellow, diamond-shaped push-pull knob
explanation: Newer vehicles use a yellow, diamond-shaped push-pull knob. The red eight-sided knob is the trailer air supply control.

prompt: How do you set the parking brakes with the yellow diamond-shaped knob?
choices: Push the knob in
Pull the knob out
Turn the knob a quarter turn
Press the brake pedal, then push the knob in
explanation: Pull the knob out to put the parking (spring) brakes on, and push it in to release them.

prompt: Why should you never push the brake pedal down when the spring brakes are on?
choices: It releases the spring brakes, and the vehicle may roll away
The springs and air pressure combined could damage the brakes
It makes the safety relief valve open and vent the tanks
It locks out the ABS until the engine is restarted
explanation: Pushing the pedal with the spring brakes on can damage the brakes through the combined forces of the springs and the air pressure. Not all systems prevent this.

prompt: What is a modulating control valve?
choices: A valve that cuts front brake pressure in half
A valve that keeps air in the tractor if the trailer breaks away
A valve that controls when the compressor pumps
A dash control handle that applies the spring brakes gradually
explanation: A modulating valve is a spring-loaded dash handle that lets you apply the spring brakes gradually, so you can control them if the service brakes fail.

prompt: How should you park a vehicle that has a modulating control valve?
choices: Move the lever all the way and lock it in place
Move the lever halfway so the brakes are partly applied
Leave the lever released and rely on wheel chocks only
Pull the lever partway, then pump the brake pedal
explanation: When parking with a modulating control valve, move the lever as far as it will go and hold it in place with the locking device.

prompt: A bus has dual parking control valves with a separate air tank. What must you keep in mind when using it to move after losing main air pressure?
choices: It refills itself from the spring brake chambers as you drive
It lets the bus be driven normally until the next service stop
Its air can release the spring brakes only a few times
It works only while the engine is shut off
explanation: The separate tank can release the spring brakes so you can move in an emergency, but it holds only enough air to do this a few times. Plan carefully, or you may be stopped in a dangerous spot.

prompt: On older vehicles, the parking brake control may be:
choices: A red eight-sided knob
A yellow diamond-shaped knob only
A foot pedal next to the clutch
A round blue knob or a lever
explanation: Newer vehicles use a yellow diamond-shaped knob. On older vehicles it may be a round blue knob or another shape, including a lever.

prompt: Truck tractors with air brakes are required to have ABS if they were built on or after:
choices: March 1, 1998
January 1, 1994
March 1, 1997
January 1, 1975
explanation: Air-braked truck tractors built on or after March 1, 1997 must have ABS. Other air-braked vehicles (trucks, buses, trailers, dollies) built on or after March 1, 1998 must have it.

prompt: What should you check to find out whether your vehicle is equipped with ABS?
choices: Check the registration card for the vehicle's GVWR
Look at the certification label for the build date
See whether the parking brake knob is yellow or blue
Compare the colors of the service and emergency air lines
explanation: Check the certification label for the date of manufacture to determine if your vehicle is equipped with ABS.

prompt: What color are ABS malfunction lamps?
choices: Yellow
Red
Blue
Green
explanation: Vehicles with ABS have yellow malfunction lamps. The low air pressure warning is usually red.

prompt: Where is the ABS malfunction lamp on a trailer?
choices: On the left side, front or rear corner
On the right rear corner, near the tail light
Only on the tractor's instrument panel
Centered above the rear doors
explanation: Trailers have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner.

prompt: On your newer truck, the ABS lamp comes on at start-up and stays on after the bulb check. What does this mean?
choices: The ABS is working normally and needs no attention
You may have lost ABS control at one or more wheels
The air pressure is below 55 psi
The parking brake is still set
explanation: On newer vehicles the lamp comes on briefly for a bulb check and then goes out quickly. If it stays on after the bulb check, or comes on while driving, you may have lost ABS control at one or more wheels. (Only some older systems keep the lamp on until you pass 5 mph.)

prompt: An older trailer was built before ABS was required. How can you check if it has ABS?
choices: Check whether its air lines are colored red and blue
Look in the cab for a yellow diamond-shaped knob
Look underneath for an ECU and wheel speed sensor wires
See whether the trailer is fitted with spring brakes
explanation: For older towed units, look under the vehicle for the electronic control unit (ECU) and wheel speed sensor wires coming from the back of the brakes.

prompt: How does ABS affect your normal braking capability?
choices: It increases braking force on every stop
It reduces braking force to protect the drums
It doubles the force of the spring brakes
It neither increases nor decreases it
explanation: ABS is an addition to your normal brakes. It does not decrease or increase your normal braking capability and only activates when wheels are about to lock.

prompt: Which statement about ABS and stopping distance is correct?
choices: It always shortens stopping distance, especially on dry pavement
It lengthens stopping distance every time you brake hard
It helps control but may not shorten the stop
It shortens stopping distance only on ice, snow, or wet roads
explanation: ABS does not necessarily shorten your stopping distance, but it helps you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking.

prompt: What is a dual air brake system?
choices: One air system with two compressors
An air system with both air and hydraulic brakes
A system with separate brake pedals for the tractor and trailer
Two separate air brake systems that use one set of brake controls
explanation: A dual air brake system has two separate air brake systems, each with its own tanks, hoses and lines, using a single set of controls.

prompt: In a typical dual air brake system, what does the second (secondary) system usually operate?
choices: The front axle brakes (and possibly one rear axle)
Only the trailer brakes, through the emergency line
Only the parking brakes on the drive axles
The service brakes on all of the rear axles
explanation: One system typically operates the rear axle brakes; the other operates the front axle brakes (and possibly one rear axle). Both supply air to the trailer.

prompt: Before driving a vehicle with dual air brakes, the compressor should build at least what pressure in both systems?
choices: 55 psi
100 psi
85 psi
150 psi
explanation: Allow time for the compressor to build up a minimum of 100 psi in both the primary and secondary systems before driving.

prompt: While driving a dual-system truck, one system's pressure becomes very low. What happens?
choices: The other system takes over, so braking is unchanged
Every wheel brake locks up at once and the vehicle skids
The front or rear brakes won't work fully, so stops take longer
Only the parking brake will still be able to stop the vehicle
explanation: If one air system is very low, either the front or the rear brakes will not be operating fully, so it will take longer to stop. Stop safely and have the system fixed.

prompt: During the engine compartment check of an air-braked vehicle with a belt-driven compressor, what should you check?
choices: Condition and tightness of the compressor drive belt
The pressure setting of the safety relief valve
The alcohol level in each brake chamber
The color coding of the trailer air lines
explanation: If the air compressor is belt-driven, check the condition and tightness of the belt during the engine compartment check.

prompt: To check slack adjusters on S-cam brakes, what should you do first?
choices: Set the parking brakes and pump the brake pedal several times
Build pressure to cut-out and hold the foot brake down
Drive forward at about 5 mph and apply the brakes firmly
Chock the wheels and release the parking brakes
explanation: Park on level ground, chock the wheels, and release the parking brakes so the slack adjusters can move. Then, wearing gloves, pull hard on each one you can reach.

prompt: When you pull hard on a slack adjuster, it probably needs adjustment if it moves more than about how far where the push rod attaches?
choices: About one-quarter inch
About one inch
About two inches
About three inches
explanation: If a slack adjuster moves more than about one inch where the push rod attaches to it, it probably needs adjustment.

prompt: What is the most common problem found in roadside inspections?
choices: Low tire pressure
Brakes out of adjustment
Burned-out brake lights
Crossed air lines
explanation: Out-of-adjustment brakes are the most common problem found in roadside inspections, so check the slack adjusters.

prompt: Vehicles built since what year have automatic slack adjusters?
explanation: All vehicles built since 1994 have automatic slack adjusters. They still must be checked.

prompt: During your inspection, you find a brake with automatic slack adjusters out of adjustment. What is the recommended action?
choices: Take the vehicle to a repair facility as soon as possible
Manually adjust it and continue on your normal schedule
Ignore it, since automatic adjusters fix themselves
Set the front brake limiting valve to "slippery"
explanation: An out-of-adjustment automatic adjuster signals a mechanical problem. Manual adjustment usually only hides the problem, so get it repaired as soon as possible.

prompt: Brake drums must not have cracks longer than:
choices: One quarter inch
One inch
One half the width of the friction area
The full width of the friction area
explanation: Brake drums (or discs) must not have cracks longer than one half the width of the friction area.

prompt: Which brake lining condition is acceptable during an inspection?
choices: Slightly loose but still covering the shoe
Lightly soaked with grease from the wheel seal
Worn very thin but with no cracks
Firmly attached, dry, and not dangerously thin
explanation: Linings must not be loose, soaked with oil or grease, or dangerously thin.

prompt: When checking the air hoses connected to the brake chambers, what are you looking for?
choices: Their color code
Ice on the glad hands
Cuts or wear from rubbing
The manufacture date stamped on them
explanation: Check the air hoses connected to the brake chambers to make sure they aren't cut or worn due to rubbing.

prompt: When testing governor cut-out, how should the engine be running?
choices: Off, with the key on
At a fast idle
At highway rpm under load
At slow idle with the clutch in
explanation: Run the engine at a fast idle. The governor should cut out the compressor at about the manufacturer's specified pressure, and the gauge will stop rising.

prompt: With the parking brake released, engine off, and no brakes applied, what is the maximum acceptable air loss for a single vehicle?
choices: Less than 2 psi in one minute
Less than 3 psi in one minute
Less than 4 psi in one minute
Less than 5 psi in one minute
explanation: With the brakes released, the loss rate should be less than 2 psi in one minute for single vehicles and less than 3 psi for combination vehicles.

prompt: With the brakes released and the engine off, what is the maximum acceptable leakage rate for a combination vehicle?
choices: Less than 3 psi in one minute
Less than 2 psi in one minute
Less than 4 psi in one minute
Less than 6 psi in one minute
explanation: Released-brake leakage should be less than 3 psi per minute for combination vehicles (less than 2 psi for single vehicles).

prompt: With the engine off and the foot brake fully applied and held, a single vehicle should lose no more than how much air in one minute?
choices: 2 psi
3 psi
4 psi
10 psi
explanation: With the foot brake held for one minute, the drop should be no more than 3 psi for a single vehicle or 4 psi for a combination vehicle.

prompt: During the applied-brake leakage test on a tractor-semitrailer, the gauge drops 5 psi in one minute after stabilizing. What should you do?
choices: Drive on, since combinations may lose up to 6 psi a minute
Repeat the test with the engine running at fast idle
Find and fix the leak first; more than 4 psi is too much
Drive on, but watch the low air warning light closely
explanation: The applied-brake limit for combination vehicles is 4 psi in one minute. More than that is too much air loss; check for leaks and fix them before driving, or you could lose your brakes.

prompt: In the applied-brake leakage test, when do you start timing the one-minute hold?
choices: The moment you first press down on the pedal
After fanning the pressure down below 55 psi
After restarting the engine and reaching cut-out
After the gauge settles from the initial drop
explanation: Once the air gauge stabilizes after the initial drop from applying the brakes, hold the foot brake for one minute and check the loss.

prompt: How do you test the low pressure warning signal?
choices: Engine at fast idle, then pull the parking brake knob out
Engine running, then open the drain valve on the first tank
Engine off, power on, then fan off air with the brake pedal
Engine off, then disconnect the trailer emergency line
explanation: Shut off the engine with enough pressure that the warning is off, turn the electrical power on, and fan the brakes. The warning must come on before pressure drops below 55 psi.

prompt: In a dual air system, the low pressure warning must come on before which tank drops below 55 psi?
choices: The primary tank only, since it feeds the rear axles
The secondary tank only, since it feeds the front brakes
The trailer's air tank, if one is connected
The tank with the lowest air pressure
explanation: The warning must come on before pressure drops below 55 psi in the air tank, or in the tank with the lowest pressure in dual air systems.

prompt: If the low air pressure warning signal does not work on a single-circuit system, what could happen?
choices: Sudden emergency braking from unnoticed air loss
The governor would never cut the compressor out
The ABS would switch itself off for the rest of the trip
The compressor would overheat and stop pumping air
explanation: Without a working warning, you could lose air pressure and not know it. In a single-circuit system this could cause sudden emergency braking; in dual systems stopping distance increases.

prompt: When checking that spring brakes come on automatically, at what pressure should the parking brake valve pop out?
choices: At exactly 55 psi, when the warning light comes on
At the manufacturer's setting, within 20-45 psi
At about 80-85 psi, the same as on large buses
At about 100 psi, when the governor cuts in
explanation: Keep fanning off the air. The parking brake valve (and tractor protection valve on a tractor-trailer) should pop out at the manufacturer's specification, 20-45 psi.

prompt: In a dual air system at operating rpm, pressure should build from 85 to 100 psi within:
choices: 15 seconds
2 minutes
45 seconds
3 minutes
explanation: With the engine at operating rpm, pressure should build from 85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds in dual air systems.

prompt: For older single air systems (pre-1975), what is the typical buildup requirement?
choices: 50 to 90 psi within 3 minutes at 600-900 rpm idle
85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds at operating rpm
0 to 125 psi within 1 minute at a fast idle
55 to 100 psi within 5 minutes at any engine speed
explanation: Single air systems (pre-1975) typically must build from 50 to 90 psi within 3 minutes with the engine at an idle speed of 600-900 rpm.

prompt: How do you test that the parking brake will hold?
choices: Set it, then rev the engine hard in a high gear
Set it, then pump the service brake pedal several times
Release it and let the vehicle roll down a slope
Set it, then gently pull against it in a low gear
explanation: Stop the vehicle, put the parking brake on, and gently pull against it in a low gear to test that it holds.

prompt: When testing the service brakes, at about what speed should you move forward before applying the brakes firmly?
choices: About 15 mph
About 5 mph
About 25 mph
About 1 mph
explanation: Wait for normal air pressure, release the parking brake, move forward slowly (about 5 mph), and apply the brakes firmly. Note any pulling, unusual feel, or delayed stopping.

prompt: On a tractor-trailer, when should the trailer air supply (tractor protection) valve pop out during the emergency brake test compared with the tractor's parking brake valve?
choices: Only after the tractor's parking brake valve pops out
At the same time as, or before, the tractor's valve
Only when the gauge reaches 0 psi
At least 20 psi after the tractor's valve has popped out
explanation: On air-operated trailers, the tractor protection valve and trailer brake valve should pop out at the same time as or before the truck/tractor valve.

prompt: During a normal stop with a manual transmission, when should you push in the clutch?
choices: As soon as you start braking
Before you touch the brake pedal
Only after the vehicle has fully stopped and the parking brake is set
Not until engine rpm is down close to idle
explanation: In a normal stop, don't push the clutch in until the engine rpm is down close to idle. When stopped, select a starting gear.

prompt: When you brake hard on a slippery surface without ABS and your steering wheels lock up, what happens?
choices: You lose steering control
The trailer jackknifes immediately
The spring brakes come on
Your stopping distance gets shorter
explanation: When steering wheels lock up, you lose steering control. When other wheels lock, you may skid, jackknife, or spin.

prompt: Only your tractor has ABS. While braking hard, you see the trailer begin to swing out. What should you do?
choices: Brake harder so the tractor ABS takes over
Apply the trailer hand valve to straighten the trailer
Let up on the brakes if you can safely do so
Steer sharply toward the trailer
explanation: With ABS only on the tractor you should keep steering control, but watch the trailer and let up on the brakes (if safe) if it begins to swing out.

prompt: In which case does the manual say you can fully apply the brakes in an emergency stop?
choices: When only the trailer, not the tractor, has working ABS
When the low air pressure warning light has just come on
When going downhill in the proper low gear
When the vehicle has working ABS on all axles
explanation: The one exception to normal braking is when you always drive a straight truck or combination with working ABS on all axles; then you can fully apply the brakes in an emergency stop.

prompt: How should you brake a tractor-trailer that has ABS?
choices: Pump the brake pedal rapidly to help the ABS work
Always press the brake pedal all the way to the floor
As you always have, using only the force needed
Use the trailer hand valve first, then the foot brake
explanation: Brake as you always have: use only the braking force necessary to stop safely and stay in control, regardless of which units have ABS.

prompt: If your ABS malfunctions, what should you do?
choices: Stop right away and have the vehicle towed
Drive normally and get it serviced soon
Use only the parking brake control to stop
Keep your speed under 20 mph until it is fixed
explanation: If ABS malfunctions you still have regular brakes. Drive normally, but get the system serviced soon.

prompt: Describe the controlled braking method.
choices: Brake as hard as you can without locking the wheels
Apply fully, release when wheels lock, then reapply
Pull the parking brake knob out about halfway
Brake lightly and steer sharply around the hazard
explanation: In controlled braking you apply the brakes as hard as you can without locking the wheels and keep steering movements very small.

prompt: While using controlled braking, you need to make a larger steering adjustment. What should you do?
choices: Release the brakes, steer, then reapply as soon as you can
Keep full brake pressure and turn the steering wheel harder
Pull out the trailer air supply knob to slow the trailer
Downshift two gears while keeping the same brake pressure
explanation: If you need to make a larger steering adjustment or the wheels lock, release the brakes, and reapply them as soon as you can.

prompt: Describe the stab braking method.
choices: Tap the brake pedal lightly several times every second
Brake fully, release when wheels lock, reapply when they roll
Hold light, steady pressure while steering to the shoulder
Pull the parking brake knob out and push it in, in short bursts
explanation: Stab braking: apply your brakes all the way, release when the wheels lock, and apply fully again as soon as the wheels start rolling.

prompt: During stab braking, why must you wait before reapplying the brakes?
choices: The compressor needs about five seconds to refill the tanks
The ABS has to reset itself before every application
The wheels need up to one second to start rolling again
The brake lights must go off before they can come on again
explanation: It can take up to one second for the wheels to start rolling after you release. If you reapply before they roll, the vehicle won't straighten out.

prompt: What is "brake lag" in an air brake system?
choices: The delay between seeing a hazard and moving your foot
The time the compressor takes to cut back in after braking
The time needed for the spring brakes to fully release
The delay while air flows through the lines to the brakes
explanation: Brake lag is the time required for the brakes to work after the pedal is pushed, because air takes time (one half second or more) to flow through the lines.

prompt: Total stopping distance for a vehicle with air brakes is made up of perception distance, reaction distance, braking distance, and:
choices: Following distance
Off-tracking distance
Brake lag distance
Sight distance
explanation: Perception + reaction + brake lag + braking distance = total stopping distance for air-braked vehicles.

prompt: At 55 mph on dry pavement, about how much distance does air brake lag add?
choices: About 6 feet
About 100 feet
About 450 feet
About 32 feet
explanation: Air brake lag at 55 mph on dry pavement adds about 32 feet. The total stopping distance for an average driver is over 450 feet.

prompt: Under good traction and brake conditions, what is the total stopping distance for an air-braked vehicle at 55 mph?
choices: Over 450 feet
About 200 feet
About 300 feet
About 150 feet
explanation: At 55 mph, for an average driver under good conditions, the total stopping distance with air brakes is over 450 feet.

prompt: What causes brake fade?
choices: Too much air pressure built up in the storage tanks
Excessive heat from overusing the service brakes
Relying on engine braking during long downgrades
Cold weather freezing water inside the brake chambers
explanation: Brakes fade or fail from excessive heat caused by using them too much and not relying on the engine braking effect.

prompt: Which two effects of excessive heat lead to brake fade?
choices: Ice forming in the valves and the governor sticking
Air lines shrinking and slack adjusters tightening up
Lining changes that cut friction, and drums that expand
Compressor oil thinning out and the safety valve opening
explanation: Heat causes chemical changes in the brake lining that reduce friction and makes the drums expand, so the shoes have to move farther and press with less force.

prompt: How do brakes that are out of adjustment contribute to brake fade?
choices: They quit early, so the other brakes overheat and fade
They lock the wheels, which keeps the drums cooler
They make the ABS shut off on that axle permanently
They raise the governor's cut-out pressure too high
explanation: Brakes out of adjustment stop doing their share before those in adjustment. The other brakes then overheat and fade, leaving too little braking.

prompt: On a long, steep downgrade, the use of brakes is:
choices: The main way to control your speed
Needed only if the vehicle lacks ABS
Not allowed except in an emergency stop situation
A supplement to the engine's braking effect
explanation: The use of brakes on a long or steep downgrade is only a supplement to the braking effect of the engine; get into the proper low gear first.

prompt: Your safe speed on a downgrade is 40 mph and you are in the proper low gear. Using the proper braking technique, what do you do?
choices: Brake steadily the whole way down to hold exactly 40 mph
At 40 mph, brake down to about 35 mph, then release
At 40 mph, brake down to about 20 mph, then release
At 30 mph, brake down to about 25 mph, then release
explanation: Apply the brakes when you reach your safe speed, hard enough to feel a definite slowdown, and release when you are about 5 mph below it. Repeat as needed.

prompt: Using the proper downgrade braking technique, about how long should each brake application last?
choices: About ten seconds
About three seconds
About one second
Until the vehicle stops
explanation: Each application, which brings speed down about 5 mph below your safe speed, should last about three seconds.

prompt: Which vehicle is MOST likely to skid out of control when its spring brakes come on from low air pressure?
choices: A heavily loaded vehicle on dry, level pavement
A fully loaded bus on a level road
A heavily loaded truck going uphill
A lightly loaded vehicle on a slippery road
explanation: Heavily loaded vehicles take a long distance to stop on spring brakes, while lightly loaded vehicles or those on slippery roads may skid out of control.

prompt: You just came down a long, steep grade and your brakes are very hot. How should you park?
choices: Chock the wheels and let the brakes cool first
Set the parking brakes right away to hold the vehicle
Set the parking brakes and pump the pedal to cool them
Leave the engine running with the transmission in gear
explanation: Don't use the parking brakes when the brakes are very hot; heat can damage them. Use wheel chocks on a level surface and let hot brakes cool first.

prompt: Your brakes are very wet and the temperature is below freezing. Why should you avoid setting the parking brakes?
choices: The wet brakes may release on their own overnight
The spring brakes will overheat while parked
They can freeze so the vehicle cannot move
The ABS will not work after the vehicle is parked
explanation: Wet brakes set in freezing temperatures can freeze so the vehicle cannot move. Chock the wheels instead, and dry the brakes by using them lightly in a low gear.

prompt: How can you dry wet brakes?
choices: Set the parking brake and rev the engine for a minute
Drive at highway speed without using the brakes
Open the air tank drains to remove the moisture
Use the brakes lightly while driving in a low gear
explanation: If the brakes are wet, use them lightly while driving in a low gear to heat and dry them.

prompt: You will be away from your truck for only a few minutes. What must you do?
choices: Nothing, if the engine is left running
Leave it in neutral with the engine off
Apply the parking brakes or chock the wheels
Hold the trailer hand valve on with a strap
explanation: Never leave your vehicle unattended without applying the parking brakes or chocking the wheels; it might roll away.

prompt: Why does the manual tell you to check brake adjustment often?
choices: Brakes can go out of adjustment quickly, especially when hot
Automatic slack adjusters loosen each time you set the parking brake
Draining the air tanks changes the adjustment of every brake
Cold brakes shrink overnight and lose their adjustment
explanation: Brakes can get out of adjustment quickly, especially when they are hot. Brakes out of adjustment stop doing their share, so the others overheat and fade.

prompt: A brake with an automatic slack adjuster is out of adjustment. Manually adjusting it should be used only as:
choices: A permanent fix for the underlying problem
A routine step at every pre-trip inspection
A temporary measure in an emergency
A way to make the adjuster last longer
explanation: Manually adjusting an automatic adjuster usually masks a mechanical problem and can give a false sense of security. Use it only as a temporary emergency measure and get the vehicle repaired as soon as possible; routine adjustment can wear out the adjuster early.

prompt: Why does a heavily loaded vehicle take a long distance to stop when its spring brakes come on from low air pressure?
choices: The ABS releases the spring brakes on heavy loads
The spring brakes do not work on all axles
The tractor protection valve keeps them half applied
The governor cuts air to the springs under heavy loads
explanation: When pressure drops to 20-45 psi the spring brakes come on, but they do not work on all axles, so a heavily loaded vehicle takes a long distance to stop. It is safer to stop while there is still air for the foot brake.
